intro: This branch is a toolkit of methods for finding integrals that the basic rules can't handle. Much of the work is recognizing which tool fits a problem.

VI.5.01.what: Substitution: spotting a function nested inside another and renaming it, so the integral becomes a simple one. It reverses the chain rule.

levels.a: Spots the inside function to rename.
levels.b: Finds how the small change in the new variable relates to dx.
levels.c: Rewrites the integral in the new variable and integrates.
levels.d: Switches back to the original variable at the end.

VI.5.02.what: Using substitution on integrals with start and end points, keeping the endpoints consistent.

levels.a: Changes the start and end points to match the new variable.
levels.b: Alternatively, switches back to x and uses the original endpoints.
levels.c: Evaluates the integral to get a number.
levels.d: Uses symmetry shortcuts for balanced (odd and even) functions.

VI.5.03.what: Recognizing integrals that produce a logarithm or an inverse trigonometry function as the answer.

levels.a: Recognizes a derivative over its function, which gives a log.
levels.b: Recognizes one over one plus x squared, which gives arctangent.
levels.c: Recognizes the pattern that gives arcsine.
levels.d: Handles stretched or scaled versions of these patterns.

VI.5.04.what: When a fraction has a top as big as its bottom, dividing first splits it into easier pieces.

levels.a: Recognizes a fraction whose top has as high a power as its bottom.
levels.b: Uses polynomial long division to split it.
levels.d: Splits a fraction into separate simpler fractions.

VI.5.05.what: Rewriting a quadratic in the bottom of a fraction by completing the square, so a known pattern appears.

levels.a: Recognizes integrals with a quadratic on the bottom.
levels.b: Completes the square to rewrite the quadratic.
levels.c: Substitutes to simplify the shifted expression.

VI.5.06.what: Integration by parts: a method for integrals of two things multiplied together. It reverses the product rule.

levels.a: Derives the formula from the product rule.
levels.b: Chooses which part to differentiate using a priority list (LIATE).
levels.c: Applies the method to find the integral.
levels.d: Applies it to integrals with start and end points.

VI.5.07.what: Using integration by parts several times in a row, including a neat trick when the integral loops back to itself.

levels.a: Organizes repeated steps with a table (the tabular method).
levels.b: Handles a power of x times an exponential.
levels.c: Handles an exponential times sine, which loops back on itself.
levels.d: Solves for the integral algebraically when it reappears.

VI.5.08.what: Integrating powers and products of trigonometry functions using identities to rewrite them.

levels.a: Handles an odd power of sine or cosine.
levels.b: Handles even powers using the half-angle identities.
levels.c: Handles powers of tangent and secant.
levels.d: Handles products of sines and cosines of different angles.

VI.5.09.what: Replacing x with a trigonometry expression to simplify square roots, guided by a right triangle.

levels.a: Uses a sine substitution for roots of a number minus x squared.
levels.b: Uses a tangent substitution for roots of a number plus x squared.
levels.c: Uses a secant substitution for roots of x squared minus a number.
levels.d: Draws a triangle to switch the answer back to x.

VI.5.10.what: Partial fractions: breaking one complicated fraction into a sum of simple ones that are easy to integrate.

levels.a: Factors the bottom of the fraction into simple pieces.
levels.b: Sets up the simple fractions with unknown numbers on top.

VI.5.11.what: Harder partial fractions, where the bottom has repeated pieces or pieces that can't be factored further.

levels.a: Sets up fractions for a repeated factor on the bottom.
levels.b: Sets up fractions for a quadratic piece that won't factor.
levels.c: Solves the resulting system of equations for the unknowns.

VI.5.12.what: Integrals that run out to infinity. Surprisingly, an endless region can still have a finite area.

levels.a: Rewrites an integral to infinity as a limit.
levels.c: Decides whether the area is finite (converges) or endless (diverges).
levels.d: Uses the known rule for one over x to a power.

VI.5.13.what: Integrals where the function shoots off to infinity at some point in the range.

levels.a: Finds the point where the function blows up.
levels.b: Splits the integral there and takes a limit on each side.
levels.d: Decides finite or endless by comparing with a known integral.

VI.5.14.what: Estimating integrals with numbers when no exact formula can be found, and judging how accurate the estimate is.

levels.a: Estimates the error of the trapezoid method.
levels.b: Uses Simpson's rule, which fits curves instead of straight lines.
levels.c: Compares the accuracy of different methods.
levels.d: Recognizes integrals that have no formula and must be estimated.

VI.5.15.what: Looking at an unfamiliar integral and deciding which method to try first.

levels.a: Simplifies or rewrites the integral before choosing a method.
levels.c: Decides between integration by parts and partial fractions.
levels.d: Uses integral tables and technology sensibly.

VI.5.16.what: The functions that undo the hyperbolic functions. They can be written using logarithms and appear as answers to some integrals.

levels.a: Writes inverse hyperbolic functions as logarithms.
levels.c: Recognizes integrals that give them as answers.
levels.d: Compares them with the similar inverse trig patterns.
